Before diving into the many meanings, here is the core idea that ties everything together:

A figure is something that has a clear, recognizable form — something you can count, see, identify, or point to. It could be a number with a definite value, a shape with a clear outline, a person who stands out, or a diagram that represents something visually. Once you feel this core idea, every meaning of figure will make immediate sense.
1. A Number or Digit

This is the most basic meaning. A figure is a written numeral — one of the digits 0 through 9. When you write the number 375, it contains three figures (3, 7, and 5).

In everyday use, this extends to mean any specific numerical amount, especially one that is official, measurable, or significant. This is why figure and number often feel interchangeable, but figure has a slightly more formal, precise feel — it suggests a number that has been calculated or measured, not just guessed.

"Write the amount in figures" means write it as digits (e.g., 500), not as words (five hundred). "The unemployment figures were released today" means the official statistical numbers were published.

A six-figure salary is a salary with six digits — anywhere between $100,000 and $999,999. Similarly, a seven-figure deal is worth between $1,000,000 and $9,999,999. This is a very common way people talk about amounts of money in English.

A ballpark figure is a rough, approximate estimate — not exact, but close enough to give you a general idea. If you ask a contractor "how much will the repairs cost?" and they say "$2,000, but that's just a ballpark figure," they mean that's a rough guess, not a firm price. "Can you put a figure on it?" means "can you give me a specific number?"
2. A Person's Body Shape

When talking about a person's physical appearance, figure refers to the overall shape of someone's body — the way their silhouette looks as a whole.

"She has a slim figure" means her body shape is slim. "He has an athletic figure" means his body looks strong and well-built. "The dress flatters her figure" means the dress makes her body shape look particularly good.

Notice that figure in this sense is not about any single body part — it is about the whole shape, the outline you see when you look at a person. It is a graceful, dignified word for body shape, which is why it is preferred in formal or polite contexts.
3. A Person (Seen from a Distance, or as a Type)

Figure can refer to a person, and this happens in two distinct ways.

As a shadowy or distant person: When you cannot see someone clearly — because they are far away, in the dark, or in dim light — you often describe them as "a figure." "A tall figure appeared at the end of the corridor." "She noticed a dark figure moving through the fog." In these sentences, the word figure captures the idea that you can see the shape of a person but not their full detail. It creates a sense of distance, mystery, or tension. The person is recognized as human, but remains somewhat undefined.

As a notable or symbolic person: This is the meaning you encounter most often in news, history, and literature. Here, calling someone a figure implies they are important, influential, or representative of something.

A public figure is someone well known to the general public — a politician, celebrity, or prominent professional. A historical figure is an important person from the past, like Gandhi or Marie Curie. A political figure is an influential person in the world of politics. A key figure in an event or movement is a central, crucial person — someone without whom things would have gone differently.

"A father figure" is one of the most useful compound uses: it refers to someone who is not your actual father but who plays that role in your life — someone older who guides you, supports you, and earns your respect and trust the way a father would. Similarly, you might hear "a mother figure," "a mentor figure," or "an authority figure" (someone who represents power or rules, like a teacher, officer, or boss).

"To cut a fine figure" means to make a very good impression — usually through your appearance, behavior, or presence. "She cut an impressive figure at the conference" means she came across as striking and admirable.

"A figure of fun" refers to someone who is routinely laughed at or not taken seriously — a person others mock or find ridiculous.
4. A Shape or Geometric Form

In mathematics and visual art, a figure is a shape with a clear, defined boundary. Circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, and pentagons are all geometric figures. This is the most purely visual meaning of the word — a figure is literally a form you can see and outline.

You will encounter this in math class: "Calculate the area of the figure" means calculate the area of the shape shown. "The figure has three equal sides" means the shape (a triangle) has three equal sides.
5. A Diagram, Illustration, or Chart

In textbooks, academic papers, scientific reports, and formal documents, figure is the standard word for any visual aid — a diagram, chart, graph, photograph, or illustration used to explain something that is difficult to describe in words alone.

You will see labels like "Figure 1," "Figure 2," and so on throughout such documents. "See Figure 3 on page 47" means look at the diagram or illustration labeled Figure 3. "Figure 1 shows the structure of a DNA molecule" means the diagram labeled Figure 1 displays this.

The logic is simple: a diagram has a clear visual form, so it is a figure.
6. A Pattern or Decorative Design

Figure can also mean a repeated or distinct decorative pattern, especially woven into or printed on fabric, wallpaper, or other surfaces.

"The silk was covered in beautiful figures" means the silk had beautiful decorative patterns on it. "The carpet featured geometric figures in blue and gold" means it had geometric patterns in those colors.

In music, a figure is a short melodic or rhythmic pattern that repeats — a musical motif. This is the same idea: a recognizable, distinct form that appears repeatedly.
7. A Set Pattern of Movements (in Dance or Skating)

In dance and ice skating, a figure is a prescribed sequence of movements performed in a set pattern.

This is exactly where figure skating gets its name. In the early history of competitive skating, skaters were judged on their ability to trace precise geometric shapes — especially figure-eights — onto the ice with their blades. Those traced shapes were the figures. The term stuck, and the sport became "figure skating" even after the tracing requirement was removed from competition.

In ballroom dancing, a "figure" refers to a specific, named movement sequence — a building block of choreography.
8. A Figure of Speech

A figure of speech is a phrase or expression used non-literally to create a vivid, dramatic, or interesting effect in language. Instead of describing something plainly and directly, a figure of speech communicates it in a creative, indirect way.

"It's raining cats and dogs" is a figure of speech — no animals are actually falling from the sky; it simply means it is raining very hard. "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse" is a figure of speech (specifically, an exaggeration called hyperbole). Metaphors ("life is a journey"), similes ("as brave as a lion"), and irony are all types of figures of speech.

When someone says "it's just a figure of speech," they are telling you not to take their words literally — they were speaking expressively, not making a factual claim. If someone says "I could kill for a coffee right now" and then adds "that's just a figure of speech!" they are clarifying that they are not making a genuine threat — they simply want coffee very badly.
How All the Meanings Stay Connected

Every meaning of figure shares the same invisible thread: something that is clearly defined and stands out from its surroundings.

A number stands out from text. A body shape is a distinct silhouette. A notable person stands out from the crowd. A geometric shape has a clear, defined boundary. A diagram is a visual form that represents data. A decorative pattern stands out on a surface. A movement sequence is a recognizable, set form. A figure of speech stands out from plain, literal language.

Once you feel this connection, the word figure will never seem like a collection of unrelated meanings. It is always the same idea: a clear, identifiable form — whether numerical, physical, visual, personal, or linguistic.
